Using 11.0 TeV data from the LHC, collected by the CMS detector, the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay rate width for the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ lifespan was calculated. The relevant data consist of reconstructed decay events from $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$, obtained through kinematic reconstruction in the diKaon mass spectrum. The effective $B^0_s$ decay rate width was determined from a maximum likelihood fit to the diKaon mass distribution of both recently observed and previously studied events. The experiment yielded the following result: $\Gamma_{\rm eff}^{B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-} = (0.443 \pm 0.026 \pm 0.013 \pm 0.016) \times 10^{-11} \, \mathrm{GeV}$, where the first error margin is statistical, the second arises from uncertainties in the simulation, and the third is due to uncertainties in the simulation of other physical processes. This allowed the $B^0_s$ lifespan to be reconstructed directly from LHC data for the first time, resulting in the following measurement: $\tau_{B^0_s} = 1.40 \pm 0.03 \pm 0.01 \pm 0.01 \,

This research focuses on a model that represents a growing network, where the size of the network is finite, and one of the nodes in the network can spread to more of its nodes in a stochastic manner. The model's dynamics are determined by the average size of the network and a time delay, and we analyze the average number of connections of a node in the network. A distributed equation that describes the average connections of a node is examined using numerical methods, and our study investigates its stability and discrete implementations in a effort to understand the network's behavior in greater detail.

At the Pierre Auger Observatory, extensive air shower events are recorded, providing a way to investigate the high-energy cosmic ray anisotropy. In order to investigate intergalactic space on a large scale, an all-sky map of extensive air shower events recorded between 2004 and 2017 is assembled, covering 80% of the sky and corresponding to 1444 days of observation. In order to track the movement of the Earth through the cosmos, the all-sky dataset is divided into four energy ranges, linked to the velocity of the Auger detector relative to the cosmic microwave background. In order to quantify the anisotropy, multipole moments are calculated using a harmonic expansion, providing a measure of the pattern of distribution. The results reveal a dipole anisotropy at extremely high energies that becomes more pronounced in the highest energy range, with a amplitude of 27.1% for E > 6.6 EeV. In order to rule out the influence of residual muons, the analysis is limited to the most energetic threshold of 6.6 EeV. In order to investigate the origin of the anisotropy, the effect of the galactic disk is modeled and compared to the data in different frames of reference, providing evidence for the direction of the local group of galaxies.

This paper provides a proof that Zinbiel algebras are strictly nilpotent, which was not previously known.  In 2012, Bae and Khoroshkin established a one-to-one correspondence between Zinbiel algebras and shuffled Lie algebras due to their compatible opposite structures.  However, since shuffled Lie algebras are universally acknowledged to be solvable, it follows that all Zinbiel algebras exhibit the same property.  This implication was also established in the referenced work.

This research investigates the fluctuations in the direction and intensity of particle flow in lead-lead collisions at the LHC, specifically at a 5.02 TeV energy level. Using a statistical approach, variations in the angle of flow are measured across 26,000 recorded collisions, revealing an average variation of 3.4 degrees and providing insights into possible influences from rare, high multiplicity events. Furthermore, correlations between the fluctuation of particle multiplicity and the fluctuation of the angle of a specific type of particles, known as protons, are discovered in both identical and opposite asymmetry forms. These findings are analyzed in relation to the shape of the LHC's collision path and the shape of the produced particle distribution.

This research focuses on resolving differences in database tables that have missing data entries. We consider two types of discrepancies: those resulting from missing data and those arising from conflicting information. For the former, we define and discuss the concept of connectivity between tables, which is essential for determining whether one table can be inferred from another. For the second type of discrepancy, we explore a more complex scenario where the relationship between variables in the tables is defined, and we define and analyze the properties of a solution to such a scenario. We also discuss the computational difficulty of determining connectivity and other related problems, and we present a method for addressing these issues that involves transforming the tables to eliminate missing data, which we prove to be computationally intensive.

Linear Poisson regression models are commonly used to analyze count data, capturing the relationship between counts and explanatory variables through a linear predictor. Count time series analysis, on the other hand, often employs autoregressive models like Poisson autoregression (PAR) to model count data without covariates by treating past observations as predictors. In situations with available covariates and historical count data, combining both elements is desirable, yet current models struggle when the coefficient of interest changes over time. To address this challenge, we have developed a novel TPAR model that integrates past observations and covariates in a linear predictor framework, enabling the modeling of count time series with temporal-varying coefficients. We have utilized the TPAR model to analyze monthly COVID-19 deaths in 20 countries, selecting the optimal model using the TPAR's order and lag selection criteria and estimating the TPAR model using a quasi-Newton method. Model evaluation and residual analysis confirm the TPAR model's adequacy, and we have made probabilistic forecasts for future counts and identified explanatory variables associated with COVID-19 deaths.

The success of recent object representation methods relies heavily on large datasets with a consistent arrangement of objects, which limits their ability to generalize when encountering new objects. Few-shot and zero-shot object manipulation tasks require models to handle object descriptions that are significantly different from the training data, presenting a substantial challenge. In this study, we introduce a novel object description format known as the Neural Description Field (NDF), which represents object surface descriptions as point clouds of feature vectors. NDFs maintain a one-to-one correspondence with object surfaces, enabling them to preserve the geometric properties of the object and provide a compact, efficient, and content-rich description. We demonstrate the effectiveness of NDFs in object manipulation tasks including zero-shot and few-shot classification, shape completion, and attribute prediction. Furthermore, we show that NDFs can be integrated into existing representation methods to achieve superior performance. The success of NDFs in handling object descriptions with diverse spatial transformations and a high level of geometric invariance is a key highlight. The source code and NDF data are available at https://github.com/andrewrs1/NDF-PyTorch.

Using the traditional $G$-$a_0$ parameters for $O(N)$ universality classes from $N=1$ to $4$, we have calculated the global position of the Yang-Lee $\sigma_1$ edge relative to the critical thermal $\sigma_2$ edge for lattice gauge fields with fixed numbers of fields. These calculations were carried out using high-precision numerical methods based on exact renormalization group theory, exact diagonalization, and scaling analysis near critical points in a four-dimensional hypercubic lattice with $L^4=64$ to $256^4$ sites and linear extensions up to 512 in linear dimension. The results show that the Yang-Lee edge is located at a ratio of $σ_1/σ_2 = 0.02461(5)$ for all $N$ values, indicating a universal behavior across different $O(N)$ universality categories.

In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to ensure that a desired estimator or maximum likelihood can be efficiently located within complicated, potentially non-convex optimization landscapes. While tools like random matrix theory and high-dimensional geometry have advanced our understanding of these landscapes theoretically, developing actionable regularity results to locate desired solutions remains a significant challenge. In an effort to address this challenge, we aim to both extend results from the analysis of spiked covariance and the study of the Approximate Message Passing algorithm, specifically by adapting the concept of "Tightening" from covariance models to the AMP framework, we introduce a new "AMP-Tightening" technique, thereby filling a notable gap in the AMP literature. This technique is particularly useful in various contexts, including the analysis of technical issues in a recent study that demonstrated the local convexity of the TAP free energy in a small neighborhood of the critical point.

Recent efforts to integrate stellar photometry data into atmospheric modeling have been compared to existing approaches for aerosol characterization using optical depth, which is currently achieved through various remote sensing techniques such as satellite imagery, lidar, and radiometry. Although the effort required to compute aerosol properties from photometry data is significantly higher than what's possible with radiometry data, a new method has been developed to streamline this process. Leveraging precomputed lookup tables, this method allows for the efficient retrieval of aerosol properties by simply inverting a connection between the measured brightness of a star and its position in a specific color space. When applied to six years of photometry data from the Kepler space telescope, this approach successfully recovered aerosol properties derived from another instrument on the same satellite, demonstrating its effectiveness and potential for large-scale aerosal monitoring using photometry missions.

To accurately estimate a robot's complete six-degree-of-freedom pose from position and orientation data, clustering-based methods have been widely adopted in recent years. To build on the strong performance of these approaches, we present two key enhancements. Firstly, we develop a clustering and projection fusion network that leverages both data types simultaneously, allowing the model to share knowledge between the two tasks and reduce the overall parameter count. Secondly, we introduce a correspondence learning framework based on the attention mechanism to further refine pose clustering results. Experiments conducted on the PR2 and Amazon palletizing datasets demonstrate our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques and provides a robust foundation for downstream tasks that rely on precise pose estimation.

We present GGLasso, a Python-based tool for Generalized Graphical Lasso
computation, which identifies the most concise representation of conditional
dependence among random variables adhering to a specified distribution. 
GGLasso supports multiple algorithms, including those developed by Friedman
(2007) and Cho and Kim (2018), and can be expanded with custom algorithms. 
The package features pre-computed demonstration data for immediate testing, 
along with extensive documentation and data visualisation capabilities for 
data scientists.

In molecular dynamics simulations, maintaining a chemically accurate bond connectivity is essential. We have developed a chemically robust molecular sampling method that consistently preserves the correct bond connectivity configuration throughout the dynamics process by utilizing an average of multiple initial temperature configurations. This new method, known as robust dynamics (Ld), has been found to match the standard dynamics (Ed) method at high temperatures and outperform it at lower temperatures where heat exchange occurs with the environment. Our research demonstrates the superiority of robust dynamics as temperatures drop below a specific threshold, making it a highly effective and efficient approach for exploring the molecular configuration through various temperature-related landscapes.

As complex systems evolve from simple to multi-layered representations, traditional methods of analysis fall short in identifying key nodes across various interactions. Our novel framework, Multi-Eigenvector Prominance (MEVP), analyzes node prominence across various layers of a complex network by integrating various eigenvector promotion methods. MEVP can isolate critical nodes that play a unified role across different interactions in the network's various layers. We tested the framework on diverse networks with deliberately introduced distortions and real-world multi-layered networks, revealing its superior performance in locating entities with combined influence, particularly in network's various interactions.

In the context of Minkowski spacetimes characterized by a non-standard metric signature, we investigate a specific operator that was first described by Dirac in 1928. This operator, initially formulated using complex numbers, is now examined using only real numbers to identify the geometric properties of its solutions. A specific configuration of the metric, where two of its components share the same distinctive signature, enables us to analytically and geometrically interpret the operator's 0-eigenspace. We find that the operator's condition equates to a constraint ensuring the conservation of a complex-valued momentum within a five-dimensional subspace of spacetime, while simultaneously enforcing the complete collapse of its orthogonal complement. A further exploration of the operator's properties, specifically its hermitian nature in the complex domain and its symmetric characteristic in the real domain, reveals that in R-Minkowski spacetimes, it defines a Lagrangian subspace.

This study investigates how spheres behave when they come into contact with a liquid surface, specifically during the initial stage of impingement. We analyzed 48 high-speed video recordings of spheres of varying sizes and at different approach speeds, and identified and categorized the main flow patterns that occur. The primary seal rupture time is defined as the time it takes for the air sphere surrounding the incoming object to break, and this time was found to be influenced by the speed of approach, with little effect from the size of the sphere. At lower speeds, a distinct flow pattern was found where the air sphere forms outside the water surface before being trapped, and this pattern disappeared at higher speeds. The speed at which spheres break the surface was found to be significantly lower than that of flat surfaces and increased more slowly with the size of the sphere. Additionally, the study observed the deformation of the water surface, which was found to be significantly greater than that of flat surfaces but showed little dependence on the size of the sphere.

In the context of Type IIB supergravity, we investigate the possible invariants that can be added to the theory, focusing on those that break U(1)R symmetry and the so-called "shift symmetry" of the axiodilaton. We identify two types of theories based on whether U(1)R is completely or partially broken. We then explore the impact of these symmetries' breaking on the effective field theories of the moduli within the 14-dimensional landscape, and we discuss how superpotential and non-perturbative corrections can be implemented in these theories. Additionally, we analyze two classes of models where the symmetries are extended, and we present scenarios where the axiodilaton can develop a non-zero vacuum expectation value through non-perturbative effects, and where it remains perturbatively massless in flux compactifications.

The transition from a band-magnetic to a correlation-driven Mott state in spin-crossover copper sulfides is an intriguing topic of study. In this paper, we investigate the gradual transition between the band-magnetic and Mott insulating states in cubanite CuFe2S3 using a combination of a tight-binding approach and the Hubbard model solved through the TRMG method. Our calculated cubanite structure exhibits magnetic properties that closely resemble experimental observations, along with correct electron occupancy and a substantial quasiparticle gap. Notably, our results reveal orbital asymmetry caused by the interplay of crystal field and Coulomb interactions, resulting in a selective filling of the $d_{x^2-y^2}$ orbital and an anomalous Hall effect. Furthermore, our study shows that cubanite exhibits orbital instability and a small but finite quasiparticle gap in the $p$-filled orbital even when the $d$-orbital is fully filled. Finally, we demonstrate the existence of a metal-insulator transition in cubanite as the plectron correlation strength increases.

The interplay between strong coupling and a high-mass Rabi frequency has been extensively studied theoretically and experimentally in the context of semiconductor physics. However, achieving massive Rabi oscillations in InGaAs quantum dots requires overcoming a significant challenge, as it demands eliminating the influence of an external magnetic field to prevent the dark exciton state from decoupling. This study investigates the dynamics of dark excitons by observing massive Rabi oscillations without an external magnetic field, and the associated physics is modeled using a modified two-level Hamiltonian with corresponding damping effects. Experimental data reveals that heavy-hole Rabi oscillations follow a $\cos$-like pattern, whereas light-hole Rabi oscillations exhibit $|\cos|$ behavior. Additionally, we find that the heavy-hole and light-hole Rabi frequencies increase linearly with the intensity of the applied microwave pulse, with higher light-hole frequencies and approximately 2.5 times greater rates of increase than their lighter counterparts. Notably, we discover that the Rabi frequencies for dark excitons are about 2.5 times greater than their spin-resolved analogues due to their unique coupling mechanism involving two heavy-holes. Our findings provide a comprehensive understanding of the unique dynamics of dark excitons and open up new avenues for further research in this area.

In two-dimensional electron lattices with non-symmorphic symmetry, the unique folding of the Brillouin zone along mirror lines creates "nodal lines" that cannot be eliminated through time-reversal and spin-orbit coupling mechanisms. This research explores how these non-symmorphic nodal lines can be manipulated by introducing a dimerization pattern along lattice lines, specifically examining a modified Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Focusing on a one-particle approximation, the study investigates the effects of breaking inversion symmetry on a "halfway line" within the line-line folded lines of the Brillouin zone. As the system's parameters are adjusted, the line of line-folded lines undergoes a transition from an insulating state to a metallic state along a line in the two-dimensional Brillouin zone, accompanied by the appearance of a line node anti-adiabatic point. Furthermore, the line node's behavior is found to exhibit semivielly-Clarke topology upon crossing a phase transition point. Notably, the study demonstrates how the line node can be closed at discrete points in space through the application of a perpendicular magnetic field, resulting in the formation of a "halfway line" semivielly-Clarke monopole. Quantum light sources, exhibiting super classical characteristics, hold immense potential for enhancing security in quantum communication protocols and improving precision in measurement and quantum sensing. One such state is the single-photon facilitated coherent state, which can be generated through quantum-optical catalysis. In this process, a non-linear crystal, activated by a strong laser field, interacts with a single photon, re-emitting it while transforming the phase space of the underlying coherent state. The intensity of the driving field plays a crucial role in determining the effectiveness of this transformation. A compact, fiber-based system has been designed and built to produce these single-photon facilitated coherent states via quantum-optical catalysis. Experimental evidence supports the confirmation of endogenous squeezing generated during this process. The experiment also demonstrates the versatility of this catalytic approach in producing a wide range of single-particle facilitated states.

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors is an interesting area to explore. We demonstrate the relevance of this choice of framework by employing Newman-Penrose tetrad fields to derive the complete linearization of the Einstein non-linear equations. This leads to a clearer interpretation of the Newman-Penrose scalar variables, particularly thePhi_{0,1,2} andPsi_{0,1,2} components. As a result, the structure of the Papapetrou identity is revealed, providing a differential identity for thePsi variables that reflects the dynamics of the electromagnetic field in accordance with the Newman-Penrose scalar representations. This identity is also recoverable from the Bianchi identities, and a specific choice of tetrad field allows for the metric's recovery from the Weyl curvature and the electromagnetic field variables.

Deduction systems have long been utilized to establish the validity of mathematical theorems and facilitate automated problem-solving. More recently, their capabilities have expanded, enabling them to process knowledge represented in natural language and derive new information. Our research focuses on employing deductive methods to derive complex structures, such as polymers, from simpler inputs like text-based descriptions and rules. By combining first-order logic with Prolog, we have developed a technique to derive a "food chain" of nutritionally related polymers. To tackle combinatorial challenges in this process, we employed dependent type theory and solved R's linear regression functions to establish an efficient solution for navigating the complexity of polymer combinations.

Segmenting tumors in the esophagus using CT scans is a challenging medical image processing task with significant implications for cancer treatment planning. The primary goal is to accurately identify and outline the tumor in the esophagus from CT images, a task made difficult by factors such as low image contrast, irregular tumor boundaries, and the presence of noise. In this study, a new deep learning-based image segmentation model called DDAUnet is introduced to improve the accuracy of esophageal tumor segmentation. The DDAUnet is based on a modified Unet architecture that includes several innovative components, a dilated convolution encoder, a dense convolution decoder, and a focus gate mechanism. The model was trained and evaluated on two publicly available datasets, and the results show that it outperforms existing state-of-the-art segmentation methods. The DDAUnet's components were found to play a crucial role in capturing long-range spatial information and local details, leading to more accurate and reliable tumor segmentation in CT scans.

This research focuses on translating social media content from English to non-English, specifically by examining the factors that hinder or facilitate NLP-based translation for this type of content conversion. Our analysis of existing and new data reveals that non-English content is more likely to be processed NLP-wise when it has clear boundaries, a larger audience, and available resources. Conversely, the size of the language community matters less when the language has a strong association with a larger, more developed country's economy. Content code-switching between languages is more likely to be processed NLP-wise than pure text in either language. Furthermore, we found that content in highly developed country-affiliated languages often includes non-English elements, whereas content in less developed country-affiliated languages is more likely to be purely in those languages. Finally, we identified that content code-switching is more likely to be processed NLP-wise when non-linking elements are used, particularly when the primary non-linked language is not English. Our study has significant implications for multilingual communities and offers directions for addressing the challenges of NLP-based translation in these communities.

As multiple human-feedback tasks have been streamlined to automate more effectively, the need for efficient and effective platforms to evaluate and enhance various techniques has increased. Although several such platforms exist, there is currently no available tool designed specifically to evaluate image descriptions generated by automated methods. In this study, we create a human annotation system called VIDIA to evaluate image descriptions generated by automated methods. We also investigate the utility of existing reference information from human annotations in improving the performance of multiple models, and find that carefully selected reference information can significantly enhance performance when compared to other forms of existing information.

Tantalum oxide (Ta$_2$O$_5$) is a technologically significant material used in semiconductor production, optical applications, and as an electrical insulator. Ta$_2$O$_5$ has an amorphous structure under normal conditions, with various crystal forms that exhibit different electronic properties. The study of Ta$_2$O$_5$'s unique electronic behavior relies heavily on its crystal structure. The paper investigates the relationship between the structure and properties of Ta$_2$O$_5$ by examining its possible crystal configurations. Researchers used a density functional theory to study the electronic properties of the material. The study discovered that the crystal forms of Ta$_2$O$_5$ exhibit semimetal and semiconducting behaviors with different band gaps. The study also found that the material behaves as a semimetal in its ground state, with an indirect band gap of 2.44 eV in its insulating state. The researchers employed the Monte Carlo method to explore the stability of the crystal forms of Ta$_2$O$_5$ by applying small random distortions to the structure. The study identified three main crystal forms of Ta$_2$O$_5$ with Ta octahedra arranged in different patterns. Spatial information plays a crucial role in the dissemination of fake news on online social media platforms. In this study, a new experimental design was implemented to investigate the specific impact of big geographic formations, such as states, on the dissemination of false news on Reddit. A unique statistical approach was developed to analyze data from this novel experiment. Findings reveal that depicting a misleading state, Texas, with an exaggerated size can contribute to the propagation of false news, a effect that is referred to as a "Texas gazebo" effect. Furthermore, a case of the Alabama hoax was discovered to have a comparable outcome to the Texas state image, a effect that is referred to as the "Alabama gazebo" effect. Conversely, when a state is drawn with its accurate proportions, a neither-nor effect was observed where neither distorted nor correct state images have a significant effect on the spread of misinformation. This study's discoveries are significant as they can be applied to map-based information systems and highlight the critical role of geographic formations in influencing the spread of misinformation, a phenomenon that is particularly prevalent and harmful in the current political climate.

Verbal guidance from human instructors through spoken instructions is a key aspect of natural interaction. Yet, it remains unclear what specific aspects of speech are essential for a robust demonstration learning system. This study investigates the acoustic characteristics of speech used during robot manipulation tasks. Comprehending these features is crucial for developing a learning framework capable of processing the full spectrum of verbal guidance provided by human instructors. We gathered a unique dataset consisting of 1,000 tasks where instructors verbally explained the demonstration of a manipulation task while interacting with a physical robot. Thorough feature analysis reveals that certain speech patterns can be associated with particular manipulation actions and that the temporal alignment between speech and action is an essential factor. These findings are validated through controlled experiments and can be utilized to create a more informed prior in a transformation model that integrates visual data and acoustic patterns for achieving a comprehensive understanding of displayed demonstrations.

The core equation governing classical field theory, regardless of dimension and spatial dimension, is expressed in a geometric format as the Hardy-Weber distribution. This is achieved by converting the Lagrangian rigidity into a more concise format. By transforming the Lagrangian's expressible nature into a Hamiltonian distribution. It is noteworthy that this conversion is not a straightforward conversion, but rather a complex transformation. Furthermore, this conversion is tied to the Euler-Arnold equations, which describe the evolution of a fluid. This is because it corresponds to the moment-and-curvature evolution of a curve, which is equivalent to the sine-Gordon equation. This is due to the fact that this conversion embodies the geometric field theory's intricacy, which is embodied by the Kummer-Matthews-Stockwell transform. This is because this translation is represented by this transformative operator.

Conversational systems are being used in conversations with humans in various fields such as customer service, news delivery, and more. Although these applications are moving forward, there's uncertainty about the performance of conversational bots in ongoing interactions due to the lack of a standardized evaluation method. To bridge this gap, we have developed a framework for assessing the efficacy of conversational bots in ongoing interactions. This framework relies on a set of evaluation dimensions and an automated process to generate test scenarios. We have demonstrated the framework's effectiveness by evaluating a recently developed multi-session conversation model. The evaluation revealed areas where the model excels and where there's room for improvement. This evaluation not only provides valuable insights for researchers working on conversative models but also establishes a solid basis for the community to assess future developments in this field.

Recommendation systems face a significant challenge due to data sparsity, a
problem exacerbated in multi-domain settings where combining data from
multiple domains yields limited gains over single-domain methods. This struggle
to effectively integrate knowledge across domains stems from varying structures
and distributions, hindering a domain's potential to benefit others. This paper
proposes a novel multi-domain recommendation framework, called
Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MSDCR), which aims to
outperform traditional single-domain methods by facilitating mutual learning
among domains. In this model, two distinct parts are developed: a
Through-Linkage Preference Enhancement segment that employs stacked
autoencoders to reconcile domain differences and a Reversible-Distribution
Cooperation segment that contrasts and cooperates among the domains to
embrace diverse information. Notably, MSDCR innovates in three key areas
compared to existing work: it tackles the multi-domain challenge through
mutual learning, it reconciles data distribution discrepancies via
autoencoders, and it integrates competition and cooperation mechanisms to
boost performance. Extensive experiments conducted on three real-world
datasets, Alia, Yelp, and Yelp2018, demonstrate the MSDCR's effectiveness,
consistently delivering superior results across various evaluation metrics in
comparison to nine baseline methods.

Recent breakthrough in optical system design is achieved by incorporating a
concave loss function, providing a desirable apodization effect. This development
is significant as it enables all-dielectric optical systems with advanced photonic
components. To concic formulations' optimization, two main approaches have been
adopted, including the integration of a hypersphere optimization method and a
multi-segment polynomial formulation. However, these methods exhibit curved boundaries
that may result in localized straight edges interfering with optical lens curvature. To overcome this limitation, we develop and examine two additional parabolic boundary formulations, namely the inverse and composite types, utilizing the Hypatia.jl package. Through comprehensive testing, the composite parabolic formulation demonstrates superior performance, facilitating an ultra-low loss all-dielectric star coupler with a -27.6 dB minimum, a 5.4 dB reduction from the current record.

Radiological quality assurance is an essential task to ensure the accuracy and reliability of cerebral MRI images. Although deep learning models have been successfully used for various image quality assessment tasks, their generalization capabilities remain limited when faced with new datasets. To address this challenge, we investigate the underlying causes of poor generalization from multiple perspectives, including data distribution shifts in protocol and site, and propose a novel framework, Conditional Framework for Quality Assurance (CoFQA), to mitigate the adverse effects of distribution shifts in protocol and site. CoFQA employs a conditional framework that adapts to new protocols and sites by fine-tuning the model with a small amount of target domain data. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in improving model performance on new protocols and sites, and reveal that our analysis provides valuable insights into radiological quality assurance from multiple perspectives.

During extreme weather events, power grids often experience outages due to the disruption of transportation networks and the failure of equipment. Private electric vehicles (PEVs) have the potential to enhance grid resilience by supplying emergency power, although managing a large number of PEVs can cause control and communication issues in critical situations. This paper investigates how PEVs can contribute to emergency response efforts and develops a novel multi-agent coordination framework that determines the optimal use of PEVs' batteries and charging equipment while minimizing equipment wear and tear. Furthermore, this framework & linearization techniques create an efficient solution to a complex optimization challenge. Numerical results demonstrate that in power system emergencies, PEVs can effectively support critical loads, yet they must be carefully managed to prevent equipment stress. Conversely, in severe outage scenarios, the coordinated operation of PEVs and generators can prevent widespread blackouts by reducing the loss of load.

In this study, we tackle a challenging problem known as multi-agent recurrent meeting, in which self-learning agents repeatedly meet to share information that benefits them in the long run. To achieve this, we introduce a novel approach utilizing a dueling drive learning mechanism that encourages agents to cooperate for mutual gain. Specifically, we design a measure of "drive" representing both individual and collective knowledge, prompting the agents to meet whenever they believe they have acquired something valuable to contribute. Notably, this strategy enables successful resolution of both cooperative and non-cooperative scenarios and facilitates recurrent knowledge exchange under various conditions. To validate these findings, we conduct extensive experiments demonstrating that our method outperforms alternative strategies in terms of meeting conditions that result in long-term benefits for the involved agents.

This research examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of GdSn$_3$, CmSn$_3$, and a series of Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ compounds ($x=0.25, 0.5, 0.75$) using a combination of density functional theory and the spin-orbit coupling within the full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method. Our findings reveal that all Gd and Cm compounds adopt the AuCu$_3$ structure type and belong to the Fm-3m space group. Notably, both GdSn$_3$ and CmSn$_3$ exhibit ferromagnetic behavior, whereas the mixed compounds show ferrimagnetic behavior. Furthermore, all these compounds are indirect semiconductors with a small indirect band gap. The calculated magnetic moments for GdSn$_3$ and CmSn$_3$ are 7.0 $\mu_B$ and 0.4 $\mu_B$, respectively. Additionally, the magnetic and total densities of states for GdSn$_3$, CmSn$_3$, and Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ display significant overlap in the Fermi level region, indicating a strong correlation between their electronic and magnetic behavior.

A new category of particles, dubbed extra-baryons and extra-mesons, was discovered at the LHC, with a production rate estimated to be between 0.00002 and 0.0002 times that of top quarks. Given the abundance of top quarks generated in the early universe, theorists have explored the possibility that these extra-baryons and extra-mesons could have contributed to the baryon asymmetry observed today. Our calculations indicate that, under certain conditions, this new category of particles could account for approximately 10 to 50 times the baryon asymmetry found in the present-day universe.

For a group G, a geometric simplicial complex K and a map $\sigma$ from the simplices in K to the elements of G, we define the group complex (K, $\sigma$). A fundamental problem is deciding whether two group complexes are equivalent through a map that preserves the structure of G and the complex K. A significant challenge with this problem lies in determining whether two map complexes (K, $\sigma$) are the same when the underlying complex is the same. A groundbreaking result by Whitehouse shows that for two such map complexes to be identical, there must be a sequence of elementary Tietze moves connecting them. Our research shows a similar relationship holds for Coxeter groups of the B type, demonstrating that two equivalent map complexes can be connected through a specific set of elementary moves, also applicable to D type Coxeter groups.

This study combines weak lensing data from four large-scale surveys, specifically the Dark Energy Survey, DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys, SDSS, and 2dF, with supernova Type Ia observations from the Pantheon catalog. By analyzing 120 lensed supernovae, researchers aimed to develop a more precise model to replace the commonly used Fisher template, which fails to account for nonlinear effects and color variation. A new, individual-based lensing amplitude parameter was defined as $\sqrt{\kappa^2+\gamma^2}$, incorporating both convergence and shear effects. Lining up the Pantheon dataset with machine learning techniques revealed a non-trivial relationship between lensing amplitude and the luminosity deviation of each supernova, demonstrating a 2.8 sigma correlation. This lensing-induced brightness variation was estimated to be 0.16 magnitudes on average, with a 0.12 magnitude standard deviation for high-redshift objects beyond z=0.5. These findings highlight the necessity of correcting lensing effects in future high-z supernova cosmology studies.

A new type of photonic structure, called T-junction hubs, is presented for improved interconnects in integrated photonic systems.  These hubs combine Y-junctions to create a T-shape with two possible paths for light transmission, offering versatility in various applications.  Using a simulation-based approach, we optimized T-hub designs to minimize backscattering and maximize light transmission.  The optimal geometry features asymmetric junction angles and merging sections to break the symmetry and reduce backscattering.  The T-hub structures exhibit high transmission rates exceeding 99% and are compatible with standard integrated photonic fabrication processes.

Convolutional neural networks have achieved remarkable success in object recognition tasks. Yet, they often struggle to grasp the contextual meaning of images. Our study investigates whether object detectors trained to identify the presence of scenes in images can learn to understand context. We define a clear, context-related target variable and conduct experiments to explore this question. Our findings show that for certain types of data, even for complex, non-linear models like ResNet-50, the detected object regions contain too much information, preventing the model from mastering the context. In contrast, for simpler models such as random forests, removing the object context does not significantly impact performance. Our research also reveals that models can simultaneously recognize objects and context when the two are distinct and well-separated. To support our claims, we provide visual evidence by altering image contents based on the model's attention patterns. Our discoveries offer valuable insights for developing more context-aware artificial intelligence. Given a smooth, compact domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ with a smooth boundary that is not necessarily closed, this paper proves a striking result for a Kirchhoff-type elliptic equation with a singular term involving the Trudinger-Moser function's $s$-th power. Through rescaling techniques and an innovative decomposition of the singular component, we establish that for any $\varepsilon > 0$ and $s \geq 1$, the non-trivial solution $u_\varepsilon$ of the equation satisfies the estimate: $$\|u_\varepsilon\| \leq \theta_s + \varepsilon^{1/2} + \varepsilon\left(\frac{1}{2\pi s}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\ln\left(\frac{\theta_s}{\varepsilon}\right)^{\frac{s}{2}} + \varepsilon^{\frac{3}{2}},$$ where $\theta_s$ is a constant that depends on $s$.

Recent research indicates that for any two probability distributions on R^n, there exist subsets A and B of R^n such that the likelihood of randomly selecting points from these subsets, which are at most unit distance apart, is significantly higher than expected. In this context, we are interested in understanding how much more likely this is in the highest concentration areas of the subsets. To address this problem in a simpler scenario where points are selected uniformly at random, we have developed an algorithm to identify subsets A and B of S^n that are at most unit distance apart. The probability of finding such subsets is related to the square root of the product of the original probability distribution.

Lukewillia and Savrauskia introduced the notion of symplectic modifications to address the difficulty of comparing the symplectic categories of different manifolds, as they are not closed under cutting and regluing along Lagrangian surfaces. To illustrate the concept, consider a symplectic manifold (M,ω) and a divisor D within it, with the relation K_D being defined as the self-intersection of a curve perpendicular to D. By utilizing the operations of blowing down and blowing up, we can obtain new symplectic manifolds from (M,ω) when  -1 < K_D < 0, denoted as (Mω,δ) and (M,ω8), respectively. Furthermore, if a Hamiltonian surface α in the manifold is blown up at a point p on α, we can obtain another symplectic manifold (Q,Ω). If the conditions are met, we can find a symplectic structure Ω in Q that results in the same symplectic category as (M,ω).

A key problem with kidney transplantation is the shortage of available kidneys, and incompatible pairs significantly worsen this issue. Although research into overcoming this incompatibility has made some progress, the majority of patients remain unable to receive transplants and must continue with dialysis. Incompatible patients have higher psychological distress, lower quality of life, and ideal acceptance of incompatible kidneys was found to be predicted by the desire for a transplant, but not influenced by knowledge of rejection risks. Furthermore, this acceptance is positively associated with psychological well-being and the desire for a transplant, and negatively associated with the perceived difficulty of finding a compatible kidney. These findings highlight the importance of ideal acceptance in kidney transplantation research and the necessity of developing strategies to improve the psychological well-being of incompatible patients and increase the desire for a transplant.

This study scrutinizes the semantic relationships between 1000 semantically related word pairs, drawn from the Loughran-McDonald polarity lexicon, by analyzing the representations of individual words. Using three different word embedding models - Word2Vec, GloVe, and CoVe - we calculate the semantic distance between each pair of related words and conduct statistical and semantical assessments. The results indicate that words associated with positive or negative sentiments can be effectively distinguished in the vector space, with notable exceptions. Notably, we identify four words with contrasting Loughran-McDonald ratings that exhibit unique semantic properties. Furthermore, our analysis reveals a stronger correlation between our calculated distances and the gold-standard distances for the financial vocabulary under study.

This research extends the superposition of signal and power transmission using waveforms at multiple frequencies, exploring the optimal configuration of multiple frequency signals transmitted through multiple waveforming antennas. A new subset of frequency signals called "equivalent single single input single output orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing" and "equivalent multiple input multiple output orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing" are defined to facilitate integrated data and power transmission. For both single and multiple waveforming scenarios, conditions are established to identify the most efficient single-frequency signal equivalent to multiple waveforming signals, which can be transmitted through a single or multiple transmitter. It is demonstrated that integrated data and power transmission can be effectively managed with single or multiple signal waveform transmission by utilizing the proposed equivalents. Simulation results further support these findings.

This research examines the evolution of a liquid-solid interface in a confined space under various Overcooling conditions. The size of a nucleation site significantly influences the process, leading to either the growth of the nucleation site into a new mass or the absorption of the nucleation site by the surrounding liquid. To simulate this process, a mixed embedded boundary/level set approach has been developed, utilizing specific numerical methods to represent the Navier-Stokes equation, the energy equation, and a level set approach for overcooling variables. The resulting numerical technique effectively handles various scenarios, including the growth and absorption of the nucleation site, as well as the release of latent heat and surface tension effects. The simulated results also demonstrate the impact of overcooling, the nucleation site size, and the enclosure size on the morphology of the nucleation site.

In repeated games where players can observe each other's choices and receive small costs for taking actions to mislead, our research reveals that rationalizable equilibria can be achieved. Notably, this result stands out as it contrasts with previous findings, which require at least one player to be given significant rewards. Our approach involves a two-phase strategy: first, players rotate through pretending to be any other player by using a specific method to deceive, and then they play according to their current role's incentives. This approach requires a minimal cost to be achieved, a requirement that can be met in various scenarios, including when the number of players is limited and the number of possible interactions between them is unlimited.

We've examined how a novel intervention method, called protective rewiring, performs in containing the spread of diseases on random graph structures. During an ongoing epidemic, both susceptible and infected individuals rewire their connections, bypassing certain links to connect with newly introduced nodes at a certain pacegamma. Our analysis of the basic reproduction number for MErdy random graphs with this specific method shows that in comparison to not using protective rewiring, protective rewiring results in fewer diseases spreading more effectively under particular conditions. Moreover, as the pace of introducing new nodes increases, we found that a massive epidemic becomes virtually impossible to occur, showing that this policy can delay or prevent a large-scale epidemic, and it also shows that this strategy may be an effective way to manage the spread of diseases while minimising harm to already vulnerable populations.

This paper proposes a systematic method for evaluating PDF set modifications by combining existing theoretical methods into a cohesive framework. The framework organizes various approaches, such as re-fitting, scanning, and tailoring, and demonstrates their application through a common example using the ROOT library. Furthermore, it provides a unified procedure for evaluating options like the "gridding technique" and "log-likelihood scanning" in conjunction with re-fitting methods. Additionally, the framework highlights the need for a standardized strategy for assessing purchased PDF set modifications to ensure high-quality customization while minimizing unnecessary computational effort.

Reinforcement learning agents often inefficiently learn from their experiences, as gained knowledge either too quickly saturates or too slowly continues without adequate learning time. Several solutions have been proposed to address this limitation, but none provide an optimal balance between the two learning speeds. Our proposed solution, Policy Variance Experience Replay (PVEX), efficiently utilizes past experiences by prioritizing information with high variance, combining slow and fast learning speeds. PVEX integrates a variance-based sample selection method into experience replay, ensuring relevant past information contributes both a small update and a large amount of data. PVEX demonstrates superior performance in multiple environments, including diverse tasks and a large-scale setting with a massive data buffer, and outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques in these scenarios.

In order to handle complex, multi-way conversations where conversations continue simultaneously across various directions, our study proposes the development of a highly-branching dialogue model. The current state of art in this field only handles simple, sequential conversations, lacking in capacity to manage complex, multi-way dialogues. In response to this issue, we created a dataset comprising over 10 hours of three-way conversations and beyond. It's worth noting that this information is now publicly accessible. Furthermore, we conducted experiments using both simple, single-person dialogue data and our complex, multi-directional conversations dataset using various models, including a language-based model and a conversational policy model. It's been discovered that utilizing our dataset enables accurate generation of complex, simultaneous conversations and that incorporating a highly-branching structure improves performance in simple, sequential dialogues.

We have developed a novel algorithm for N-body simulations in a general type of modified gravity theory known as $f(R)$ gravity. This algorithm allows for rapid simulations of complicated galaxy formation simulations that include detailed simulations of star and black hole formation. In these simulations, the gravitational behavior is modeled based on how matter is clustered on different scales. Our method is highly efficient and allows for rapid testing of competing models of $f(R)$ gravity in detailed simulations that also include the formation of stars and black holes.

Building on Schramm's multiple stochastic Loewner evolution model, we establish a connection between conformal maps and Gaussian free fields in two dimensions. A specific choice of parameters in the multi-SLE model creates a linkage to the natural embedding of the Gaussian free field, thereby demonstrating that certain image sets of the two-dimensional Gaussian free field have zero capacity. Bases for further research in this area are provided.

In scientific disciplines, collaborative research is becoming increasingly common.  For collaborative projects, it's essential to have organized and up-to-date documentation, including documentation that can be easily edited and updated by multiple people with access.  In our research group, we've been using a Mediawiki-based system for some time to keep our documentation, and we've developed a template for MediaWiki pages that ensures a consistent layout and style.  We've shared these working pages' source files on a code repository, and as a result, we've created a CodeWiki that mirrors the structure of the wiki and provides the source code's documentation.  In this presentation, we'll share our experience with WorkingWiki, a Mediawiki-based platform for collaborative research, and provide the template we've used for our projects in astrophysics and cosmology.

The reaction of a turbulent jet fire to acoustic stimulation in a linearized framework has been modeled directly, bypassing perturbation approaches. The Active Flame Protocol has been adapted for jet fires and applied to estimate the specific acoustic impedance and reactance of a jet fire in a laboratory pipe. Despite the jet fire's complex and turbulent nature, its impedance matches the pipe's characteristic resistance, indicating minimal sound reflection and the absence of straining. spectral analysis reveals two distinct frequency ranges that influence reactance: a lower range shaped by jet velocity variations and a higher range influenced by vortex shedding frequencies. The influence of jet velocity fluctuations on sound reflection has been quantified through the combination of CFD simulations and an acoustic model, revealing the origin of the relevant frequencies and the spatial distribution of relevant vortex shedding frequencies. Furthermore, the impact of jet fire turbulence on sound reflection has been highlighted.

This research builds on a research technique that uses functional genomics data to identify associations between groups of genes and human traits across the entire genome. By analyzing 18 human traits in 18,441 individuals and androgen receptor expression in the liver, we identified previously unreported traits associated with androgen receptor expression in the liver and localized genetic factors for other traits. Moreover, machine learning models using functional genomics data outperformed random prediction and identified traits previously unreported for eight of the studied traits. Moreover, cross-study comparisons using mouse and human data revealed traits previously unreported for eight traits located in NEDD8 gene region and two additional traits in the FGFRL1 gene region. Moreover, androgen-related studies in literature were examined in relation to androgen receptor expression in the liver, and models using functional genomics data were related to the distribution of p-values from previous studies. Ultimately, a useful framework for identifying associations between genes and human traits across the entire genome is androgen expression in the liver is associated with kidney failure and liver cancer, and further research is needed to confirm these findings.

In recent years, research into tiny systems produced in lead-lead collisions at the LHC has gained prominence. Initially considered an extension of AuAu studies at RHIC, it is now seen as a distinct and significant area of study. This shift in perspective is supported by several key elements: the absence of initial copious gluons in these tiny PbPb systems, the limited impact of collective behavior, and the early formation of the quark-gluon plasma, which could potentially give rise to unique signals. Such early formation in tiny systems may leave observable imprints that are not present in smaller proton collisions. This paper aims to explore the challenges and opportunities in investigating tiny systems, and how they could provide crucial insights into the early stages of quark-gluon plasma formation.

The recurring emergence of neutron star binary systems in a quiescent state suggests their repeated accretion of material from their companion stars within the same region of space. By calculating the recurrence rate for random events based on probability theory, we determined that the interval between occurrences for a single system ranges from 10^3 to 10^6 years, depending on the probability of material redistribution in space. Observations of repeated outbursts from dormant X-ray binaries in the Galactic Centre support this hypothesis. We found that 90% of these systems have an interval between bursts between 10^4 and 10^6 years, with the exception of HMXB Sgr A* East, which has experienced two outbursts in 1974 and 1981. Based on their luminosity during a bright outburst, we hypothesize that these systems likely contain accreting neutron stars.

Molecular electrons experience slight oscillations caused by vibrational movements within the molecule. These movements lead to three types of scattering processes: electron-vibrational, phonon emission, and virtual-phonon processes. Within linear molecules, the electrons' perpendicular momentum leads to additional momentum-conserving requirements for these processes. This results in the formation of permanent electric dipoles through the virtual-phonon process, the modification of effective mass and magnetic moments via phonon emission, and the generation of effective potentials and coupling between spins via the virtual-phonon process. These effects are unique to linear molecules and are not observed in non-linear molecules.

In our investigation of how language understanding evolves through conversation, we delve into the underlying causes of semantic change during discourse using Natural Language Inference (NLI). By employing NLI tasks, we examine how the plausibility of a hypothesis based on a premise varies during a conversation about the same topic. Our findings reveal three types of semantic variation: referential enhancement, where the hypothesis's specificity increases; inferential enrichment, where the context provides additional information not explicitly stated; and conversational elaboration, where the hypothesis gains detail through the exchange of information. The three cases of NLI shifts we discovered can be connected to broader phenomena of semantic variability in discourse. Our work contributes to research on the interconnectedness of language understanding and conversational dynamics, and suggests a pathway for integrating Conversation Understanding models with the broader CUI continuum.

Our numerical model for rotating brown dwarfs and giant gas planets reaches the maximum possible rotation rate accurately, with better precision than its predecessor. The algorithm used to solve Maxwell's equations in our simulation is more efficient and reduces computational costs. The added precision in our rotational dynamics calculation allows us to achieve accurate results with less computational effort. The dataset generated by the simulation can support future exoplanet and brown dwarf analysis, offering parameters useful for interpreting upcoming observations from telescopes like JWST. The condition of mass-shedding limits for rotating objects is characteristic of substellar entities and cannot be replicated by simple fluid models. This in turn affects exoplanet parameters, as mass-shedding limits vary for rotating objects and should be considered when analyzing external signals from planets around distant stars. The maximum rotation rate for Jupiter is calculated to be approximately 3.7 times faster than its current rotation rate, while rotation rates for ultra-short-period exoplanets are found to be well within the mass-shedding threshold. The computational costs for the simulation are also broken down in the study.

This research explores how external force information can be incorporated into likelihood calculations for star-like outliers in high-dimensional data. A key challenge in preparing data for analysis is converting image points into a format that accurately reflects actual observed data when the amplitude of outliers is adjusted in a likelihood function. A simple approach, involving the conversion of image data into units of likely detection, was examined and refined to enhance its effectiveness in assessing the impact of high-dimensional anomalies. A variational deconvolution process was used to compare this method with other assessment techniques on both artificial and real world data sets. The results show that modifying existing estimates of high-dimensional data can lead to more accurate classification of data sets when faced with significant imbalances in anomaly representation.

Dynamical evolution of astrophysical phenomena is thoroughly examined in our study, with focus on GRB afterglows and their underlying particle acceleration mechanisms.  A previously introduced universal afterglow diagram emerges as a powerful predictive tool, offering guidance for potential discoveries.  However, certain ambiguities and conflicting theories regarding particle acceleration and radiative processes are explored in this research.  These conflicting models are systematically categorized and analyzed, with emphasis on their impact on the universal afterglow diagram.  By representing each model as a distinct region within this diagram, we facilitate a more intuitive visualization of possible future observations and their interpretative challenges.  Ultimately, our research highlights the enduring mystery of particle acceleration in extreme environments and the critical role of upcoming observational capabilities in resolving these ambiguities.

Given any graph G and a specific parameter k, we can efficiently find two subgraphs M1 and M2 within G such that they are disjoint, their union recreates G, and both have a bounded size of at most 2^(2^O(k)) times a polynomial in k, alongside the property that G has no complete subgraph of size k+1. As a consequence, we can achieve an algorithm for the Hitting Set problem with a runtime of O(2^(2^O(k)) * log^3(k)). Moreover, we can distinguish between graphs that are not containing a complete subgraph of size k+1 and those that are not the union of two specified size cliques with a 2^(2^O(k)) * poly(k) time framework.

This research aims to develop more robust and energy-efficient bipedal locomotion by incorporating propulsion assistance. To achieve this, a novel hybrid dynamical system is proposed, combining a underactuated double pendulum with a propulsive degree of freedom. By exploiting the system's non-conservative, non-Newtonian effects, we seek to create sustained, energy-enhancing limit cycles in both legs, leading to efficient walking cycles. Moreover, the high stiffness associated with this approach is believed to contribute to the resilience and ground-reaction forces necessary for sustained, ground-based locomotion. To investigate these concepts, a comprehensive mathematical model of the proposed double-leg system is created, along with controlled physical prototypes that demonstrate successful walking cycles and significant reductions in energy loss.

Given a number field K, an element f within K is classified as respected if it is integrated into the multiplicative group of K and its localization at every prime is also respected. The collection of respected elements forms a subring of the algebraic integers of K. Recent research has focused on K where this subring maintains specific algebraic properties. Recently, H. Kim and S. Park discovered that the subring of respected elements for K contains a unit group equivalent to itself when K is the field of rational numbers, yet this is not the case for certain quadratic fields. In this research, we investigate the subring of respected elements specifically for abelian fields and discover that this subring has the same algebraic properties as the original ring when K is the 6th root of unity field or its specific extensions, but this is not true for other abelian fields.

Hypervisors are commonly used in many applications, including virtual data centers, network testing, education, and security research.  However, one critical issue that has not received much attention is the reduction in CPU performance experienced by guests when CPU throttling control is enabled.  We discovered that, despite various throttle control mechanisms, widely used hypervisors fail to properly disable throttling control and do not account for the performance loss caused by CPU frequency scaling.  As a result, researchers and security professionals who rely on time-dependent operations may encounter unanticipated slowdowns.  Our studies revealed that a general hypervisor bug and two specific library issues lead to as much as a 9 GHz or 900 times performance decrease in typical applications.  Moreover, we demonstrate that the ThrottleGuard system can automatically detect and mitigate these problems by monitoring hardware performance counters and adjusting CPU frequencies in real time, ensuring consistent performance of time-sensitive experiments.  ThrottleGuard can be implemented in any hypervisor with a maximum overhead of 0.01% to 0.04%.  Our research highlights the significance of performance stability in time-dependent security research and provides a practical tool for enhancing the reliability of such research.

In our study, we take the established unknotting method for traditional knots and apply it to traditional links, uncovering a similar but distinct result. Our finding indicates that for a traditional link composed of two unknotted and unlinked components, at least one of which forms a trivial knot, at least one of the link's crossings can be erased without altering its knot equivalence. This leads us to conclude that for any unknitted traditional link, there exists at least one removable crossing that maintains the link's unknotted status.

We've established a connection between the Fox-Hatcher loop within the figure eight knot complement and Vassiliev invariants of character varieties for $SL_3(\mathbb{R})$, finding that the Fox-Hatcher loop corresponds to a specific Vassiliev invariant of filter order three. Furthermore, under the isomorphism between Vassiliev invariants and differential equations for character varieties, this loop maps to a non-trivial invariant under geometric variation.

A study was conducted to examine the tactical collaboration capabilities of a group of resource-constrained robots with limited computation and communication capabilities. The research analyzed the capacity of these robots to work together effectively in order to overcome challenging scenarios, specifically a variation of the multi-agent prisoner's dilemma game. The study required the development of a neural network architecture and tactic set to facilitate tactical collaboration among the robots, as well as the optimization of these components to maximize their joint performance. The results demonstrated that a neural network architecture could be optimized to enable these robots to effectively collaborate, leading to improved outcomes in terms of maximizing their collective rewards. The research also provided evidence of the benefits of tactical collaboration over individual decision-making, although the magnitude of these benefits varied depending on the degree of constraint placed on the robots. Overall, the study provided valuable insights into the potential for tactical collaboration to enable a conventional network of robots to tackle complex and challenging situations.

This work examines two privacy risks associated with federated learning systems from a practical standpoint.
In these scenarios, an outside attacker, given access to the learning server, leverages a model's predictions to reconstruct part of a participant's training data.
We present methods to prevent this, and also provide retraining techniques to reverse the privacy assault and restore the learning model's effectiveness.
Our approach to addressing these issues has been explored through both synthetic and real-world data sets, and the results of this research reveal that 100% of a participant's exposed data can be recovered with a learning model of comparable accuracy to the original, even in complex settings.

Traditional kernel methods rely on Bessel functions for kernel estimation, providing a consistent approach with theoretical guarantees. However, their high computational cost limits large-scale application due to Bessel functions' non-fast Fourier transform compatibility. In response, a new method called Pseudo Random Fourier Kernel Estimation (PRFKE) is proposed, estimating a consistent kernel using pseudo random Fourier attributes. Although not Bessel functions, the PRFKE's persistent similarity to them provides a persistent similarity consistency guarantee. Additionally, PRFKE benefits from the computational efficiency of the fast Fourier transform, enabling a 1000x speedup for a 256x256 input. The method also introduces a new, computationally efficient dropout variant for enhanced generalization performance. Empirical evaluations on multiple datasets demonstrate PRFKE's superior accuracy compared to the RandFour kernel and other state-of-the-art kernel methods, including the BPH kernel.

This research aims to integrate a $\frac{1}{3}$-Cartan group into a Garland product with curvature $\kappa \in (-\frac{1}{9}, 0)$ through the construction of a SCART decomposition, incorporating a Cartesian decomposition as an initial step. By incorporating a Cartesian piece with dimensionality $d=3$, we are able to insert the group via a second layer of star decomposition, ultimately achieving the desired integration.

We prove a novel M\"obius curvature property of compact conformally smooth hypersurfaces in the sphere S(n+1). Specifically, we show that if a hypersurface $\Sigma$ in S(n+1) has no singular points under its M\"obius transformation $\Theta(\Sigma)$, then its M\"obius scalar curvature $\mathcal{R}$ must be strictly positive. This positivity holds true for a class of hypersurfaces in S(n+1) that are defined by their conformal structure and divergence-free second fundamental form.

Next-generation wireless networks will offer diverse services through simultaneous information and power transfer (SWIPT), enabling devices to harvest energy from transmission signals while storing excess in a capacitor for operation. To achieve this, such devices have a large signal processing requirement due to the simultaneous retrieval of information and energy from the same channel. This paper investigates an SWIPT multi-access channel where multiple users receive signals at a massive scale, and one user stores excess energy in a finite capacitor. The goal is to maximize information rates for users with infinite capacitors and a minimum rate for the user with a finite capacitor. To manage the massive computation, we focus on a massive IoT SWIPT multi-access channel and develop efficient resource distribution algorithms that account for capacitor sizes and SWIPT computation overhead. Numerical results demonstrate significant computation savings and improved rates for users with infinite capacitors compared to existing methods.

The Cayley graph represents the symmetry group of a regular structure, with its size determined by a parameter q. A key property of this graph is its high transitivity of rank 2, indicating that any pair of points can be mapped to any other pair through an transformation within the group. However, when considering the average shortest path between randomly selected nodes, referred to as the graph's "world-smallest world" (WSW), its expected value cannot be an integer and varies across different Cayley graphs. Notably, for a large portion of values for q, the distribution of WSW values follows a power-law distribution, demonstrating the diverse structural characteristics of Cayley graph ensembles.

The detection sensitivity of gravitational wave detectors in the high-frequency range is limited by the motion of test masses, which are limited by thermal noise. A proposed method to enhance responsiveness to high-frequency signals is the "sloshing Sagnac interferometer," which uses a network of suspended interferometers in a triangular configuration. The sloshing configuration decouples the mirrors' motion from the incoming signal and allows the detection of certain gravitational wave modes that are inaccessible in traditional Michelson and Sagnac setups. Theoretical analysis and comparison with other configurations demonstrate the sloshing SN2 configuration's improved responsiveness to high-frequency signals, with some modes showing a 10x improvement over the standard setup. The sloshing design is relatively straightforward to implement by adding a few beamsplitters and phase shifters, with potential implementations being feasible for current detectors.
